summary: Registers a trace field clause for email that records transitions between handling queues or processing states. Examples include quarantining a message, mailing list moderation, timed delivery, queuing for analysis, or content conversion, whether inside one host or between hosts. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When a letter moves through a post office, stamps show where it sat. This memo adds a stamp for when an email is put aside, checked, or changed.

questions: how to record email handling states in received headers
what is the received header state clause
what does state quarantine mean in email headers
subtitle: A small addition to the Received header that says when an email was put aside, and why.

tldr.problem: Email trace fields can show big time gaps between hops, and nothing says whether the gap was a technical hiccup or a deliberate hold such as quarantine or list moderation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6729 registers an optional state clause for the Received header field, followed by one keyword such as quarantine or moderation, that marks a message entering a special handling state.
tldr.outcome: Anyone reading the trace can tell that a delay came from extra processing rather than from a transient failure. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Keywords defined
facts.value: 9 (auth, content, convert, moderation, normal, other, outbound, quarantine, timed)

facts.label: Default meaning
facts.value: normal, when no state clause is present

today: RFC 6729 is a Proposed Standard from September 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the state trace clause.

sections.title: Why Trace Fields Need Handling States
sections.content:
Email trace fields, most commonly the Received header field, record an audit trail of the path a message takes. One field is added each time the message moves from one host to the next. The SMTP specification, RFC 5321, notes that the most important use of these lines is debugging mail faults.

Sometimes there is a large time gap between two trace fields. A transient communication problem is one possible cause, but so are policy decisions: a quarantine, content analysis, authorization checks on some identity, or a mailing list server that holds mail from non-subscribers for moderation. RFC 6729 registers an optional clause so that a trace field can say a message entered such a special queue or state, letting a reader tell the two kinds of delay apart.
sections.plainLanguage: If a package arrives days late, you want to know whether the truck broke down or someone held it on purpose. This memo lets the mail system write that down.

sections.title: How the State Clause Is Used
sections.content:
The clause is called state. A Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) or other handling agent MAY use it when creating a Received field, and it is followed by a single keyword. The presence of the clause marks the message entering that state, and a later trace field added by the next agent implies it left.

An MTA implementing the specification SHOULD add a Received field when it places a message into a special handling condition, and when it decides no special handling is needed and prepares the message for relay. It does not need a separate field for the normal handoff if it has already added one for another reason. If one MTA runs a message through several special conditions, it MAY add a field for each.

The RFC walks through a message injected into MTA-1 and relayed through MTA-2 to MTA-3. MTA-2 adds a field using the new clause when atypical handling begins, then relays the message to MTA-3 when the handling completes.

The clause is not for attaching metadata such as 'is spam' or 'was converted from 8-bit to 7-bit'. Its sole purpose is to show where in the chain of custody the message was handled outside normal routing and queuing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each post office writes a note only when it sets your letter aside. The next office's stamp shows the letter got moving again.

sections.title: The State Keywords
sections.content:
Nine keywords are defined, and extensions may register more:

  • auth: queued pending authentication of some identifier in the message.
  • content: queued pending content analysis, such as spam or virus scanning.
  • convert: queued pending content conversion.
  • moderation: held for mailing list moderator action.
  • normal: not in an administrative hold, queued for or being handed to the next agent. This is the default meaning when no state clause is present.
  • other: held for reasons not covered by other keywords and not for transient technology issues.
  • outbound: placed in a queue for outbound relaying, typically the last case added on a single host.
  • quarantine: held in an isolation queue pending operator action for local policy reasons.
  • timed: held to meet a requested delivery window, such as the one in RFC 4865.
sections.plainLanguage: Each keyword is a reason on a sticky note: 'being checked', 'waiting for a person to approve', 'waiting for the right delivery time', and so on.

sections.title: Clause Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar is given in ABNF. The clause is the word state, folding white space, a queue state keyword, and optionally a slash and a value. The keyword is either one of the registered ones or an additional keyword that MUST be registered with IANA. Both the keyword and the value are MIME tokens, with FWS and CFWS taken from RFC 5322 and token from RFC 2045.

The optional value gives an extra label explaining the transition. The examples in the RFC are convert/unicode2ascii, moderation/not-subscribed and quarantine/spam. An agent MAY also add header field comments for more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is the word 'state' plus one reason word, and you may add a small extra label after a slash.

sections.title: Restraint and Granularity
sections.content:
Agents are not expected to support every state. Recording all of them could make a message header inordinately large. An agent is encouraged to annotate when a message enters a queue where a significant condition occurs or significant extra delay is possible, and especially at a handoff between independent agents.

If one system process does authentication, virus and spam scanning and queuing in a single pass, adding four fields would be unusual and extremely verbose. The RFC says the method SHOULD NOT be used that way except when analyzing a single component for performance problems. Instead, an agent SHOULD add a single annotated field showing when it finished with the message and the final disposition relative to that agent.

Finer granularity is possible, for example at transitions between an MTA operator and a Mailing List Manager operator. There is a catch: MTAs may count Received fields to detect routing loops, so a message with too many of them might wrongly be judged to be looping and be removed from the mail stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not stamp the letter at every tiny step. One stamp per post office that says what finally happened is enough, or the envelope fills up.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC adds the state clause to the Additional-registered-clauses sub-registry of the MAIL Parameters registry created by RFC 5321, and creates a new Registered-states sub-registry for the keywords.

New keywords are registered on a First Come, First Served basis under the rules of RFC 5226. Changes to existing entries are limited to the original registrant or IESG approval. Each registration gives a name, a description, a specification and a use value of current, deprecated or historic. Discussion on an email-related IETF mailing list is encouraged, with ietf-smtp@ietf.org suggested. Only queue state keywords belong in the registry, not the secondary information in the value part.

The initial set is the nine keywords above, each marked current.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of allowed reason words. Anyone can ask to add a new one, and the list marks each as in use, discouraged, or old.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A shows two Received traces. In the first, a message passes through two hosts with no extra handling, and the fields are ordinary.

In the second, a message from internal.example.com to a mailing list hosted at newyork.example.com is held for moderation. The earlier field carries state moderation (sender not subscribed), with the comment giving the real cause of the hold. The next field, added by the following host, is stamped more than an hour later (17:19:08 versus 18:33:29), which is the gap the clause explains.
sections.plainLanguage: One letter goes straight through. The other waits over an hour in a pile, and its note says 'waiting for approval because the sender is not on the list.'

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. Trace information of this kind can reveal hints about the local policy in effect when a message was handled, for example that a message was quarantined. Further discussion of trace field security is in Section 7.6 of RFC 5321.
sections.plainLanguage: A note saying 'held for checking' tells readers a little about the post office's rules, so the writer should know that.
